explanations.answer: They gain property and grow greatly in number
explanations.explanation: That's the report, friend. The Israelites settled in Goshen, "acquired property there and became fruitful and increased greatly in number." (Genesis 47:27) A family that started with one old man and his sons is now spreading out and filling up the region. I've had batches that rose less than that.

explanations.answer: They lose their flocks and scatter across Egypt
explanations.explanation: Not here, friend. The text says they settled in Goshen, got property, and grew "fruitful and increased greatly in number." (Genesis 47:27) Nobody is scattering and nobody is losing a thing. This is a family that's settling in and spreading out.

explanations.answer: They pack up and head back to Canaan
explanations.explanation: Not yet, friend. In this verse the Israelites settle in Goshen, in the land of Egypt, and they gain property there. (Genesis 47:27) They aren't packing a single bag. They're growing greatly in number right where they are.

explanations.answer: Bury him with his fathers outside Egypt
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Jacob says, "Do not bury me in Egypt, but when I lie down with my fathers, carry me out of Egypt and bury me with them." (Genesis 47:29-30) He wants to rest with his family, not in the land where he's spent his last seventeen years. That's a big ask, and he's asking his son.

explanations.answer: Bury him in Goshen among his people
explanations.explanation: Close to home, but no. Goshen is where his family lives, yet Jacob says plainly, "Do not bury me in Egypt." (Genesis 47:29) Goshen sits in the land of Egypt, so it's out. He wants to be carried out of Egypt to lie with his fathers.

explanations.answer: Bury him wherever Joseph thinks is best
explanations.explanation: Jacob doesn't leave this one open, friend. He tells Joseph exactly what to do: "Do not bury me in Egypt, but when I lie down with my fathers, carry me out of Egypt and bury me with them." (Genesis 47:29-30) That's a clear request, not a suggestion box. Joseph has his instructions.
Not quite, friend. Joseph does say, "I will do as you have requested." (Genesis 47:30) But Jacob isn't done. He says, "Swear to me," and Joseph swears to him. (Genesis 47:31)

Right, friend. Joseph says, "I will do as you have requested," and that's a solid answer. (Genesis 47:30) Jacob still comes back with, "Swear to me." (Genesis 47:31) So Joseph swears, and his word gets put on the record twice.

That's right, friend. After Joseph swears, the text says "Israel bowed in worship at the head of his bed." (Genesis 47:31) He's weak, and he's still worshiping. I'd call that a man who knows who to turn to.

It's true, friend. Once Joseph swears, "Israel bowed in worship at the head of his bed." (Genesis 47:31) He's near the end of his life, and he spends this moment in worship. Quite a sight at the head of that bed.

Not this time, friend. When Jacob hears that Joseph has come, "Israel rallied his strength and sat up in bed." (Genesis 48:2) He's ill, but he pulls himself up to meet his son. I couldn't do that before my morning cookies.

That's right, friend. The text says "Israel rallied his strength and sat up in bed." (Genesis 48:2) His father is ill, but he sits up for Joseph anyway. Somebody pulled himself together for this visit.

That's the word, friend. God told Jacob He would give the land "to your descendants after you as an everlasting possession." (Genesis 48:4) Jacob won't be the one living in it. The promise reaches past him to the family that comes after.

Not servants, friend. The promise was for Jacob's "descendants after you as an everlasting possession." (Genesis 48:4) It's about his family line, the ones who come after him. The land is promised to them.

Not the neighbors, friend. God said He would give the land "to your descendants after you as an everlasting possession." (Genesis 48:4) It stays in the family line. Jacob's descendants are the ones it's promised to.

explanations.answer: They will be counted as Jacob's own sons
explanations.explanation: You've got it, friend. Jacob says Joseph's two sons born in Egypt "shall be reckoned as mine; Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine." (Genesis 48:5) He's taking his grandsons in as his own. That's a promotion nobody saw coming.

explanations.answer: They will serve their uncles in Canaan
explanations.explanation: Not at all, friend. Jacob says the boys "shall be reckoned as mine; Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine." (Genesis 48:5) He's treating them like his own sons, not like helpers. The text says nothing about serving anybody.

explanations.answer: They will stay behind in Pharaoh's house
explanations.explanation: No, friend. Jacob doesn't mention Pharaoh's house at all. He says, "Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, just as Reuben and Simeon are mine." (Genesis 48:5) These boys are being claimed by their grandfather.

Yes, friend. Jacob says, "Any children born to you after them shall be yours." (Genesis 48:6) So Ephraim and Manasseh get counted as Jacob's, and later children stay Joseph's. They'd be called by the names of their brothers in the territory they inherit.

It's true, friend. Jacob says, "Any children born to you after them shall be yours." (Genesis 48:6) Only Ephraim and Manasseh get reckoned as his. Any later children stay Joseph's, and they're called by the names of their brothers in the territory they inherit.

That's the spot, friend. Jacob says, "I buried her there beside the road to Ephrath" and adds that Ephrath is Bethlehem. (Genesis 48:7) He says it was to his sorrow, so I think this memory still weighs on him.

Machpelah is a burial cave where Abraham, Sarah's husband, buried her (Genesis 23:19). But Jacob says he buried Rachel "beside the road to Ephrath." (Genesis 48:7) She was laid to rest along the road, not in a cave.
Bethel does have an oak. Deborah, Rebekah's nurse, was buried under it (Genesis 35:8). But Jacob says he buried Rachel "beside the road to Ephrath," which is Bethlehem. (Genesis 48:7)
That's right, friend. The text says "Israel's eyesight was poor because of old age; he could hardly see." (Genesis 48:10) That detail matters later in the story. Hold onto it.
It's true, friend. The text says "Israel's eyesight was poor because of old age; he could hardly see." (Genesis 48:10) That's why he asked, "Who are these?" Hold onto that detail.

That's the word, friend. Israel says, "I never expected to see your face again, but now God has let me see your children as well." (Genesis 48:11) He gets Joseph back, and then a bonus. I think that's a very full heart.
Not the wife, friend. Israel says, "God has let me see your children as well." (Genesis 48:11) The boys are who he's talking about. The text doesn't mention Joseph's wife in this moment.

No officials in this one, friend. Israel says, "I never expected to see your face again, but now God has let me see your children as well." (Genesis 48:11) It's a family moment. Just a grandfather and his grandsons.

explanations.answer: He crosses his hands and puts his right on Ephraim
explanations.explanation: That's what happened, friend. Israel "stretched out his right hand and put it on the head of Ephraim, the younger; and crossing his hands, he put his left on Manasseh's head." (Genesis 48:14) Manasseh was the firstborn, and Joseph had lined things up carefully. Israel crossed his hands anyway.

explanations.answer: He puts his right hand on Manasseh's head
explanations.explanation: That's how Joseph lined it up, friend. But Israel "stretched out his right hand and put it on the head of Ephraim, the younger; and crossing his hands, he put his left on Manasseh's head." (Genesis 48:14) The hands cross. Joseph set up one plan and Israel did another.

explanations.answer: He has Joseph swap the two boys around
explanations.explanation: Israel doesn't move the boys, friend. He moves his own hands: "crossing his hands, he put his left on Manasseh's head." (Genesis 48:14) His right hand lands on Ephraim, the younger one. The boys stay right where Joseph put them.

That's right, friend. Israel says, "may they be called by my name and the names of my fathers Abraham and Isaac, and may they grow into a multitude upon the earth." (Genesis 48:16) Both parts are in the blessing. Nice and full.

It's true, friend. Israel says, "may they be called by my name and the names of my fathers Abraham and Isaac, and may they grow into a multitude upon the earth." (Genesis 48:16) Both pieces are in there. The name part comes first.

explanations.answer: This one is the firstborn so put your right hand on him
explanations.explanation: That's what he said, friend. Joseph says, "Not so, my father! This one is the firstborn; put your right hand on his head." (Genesis 48:18) Manasseh is the firstborn, so Joseph speaks up for him. I think he figures his dad just made a mistake.

explanations.answer: Your eyes are tired so let me guide your hands
explanations.explanation: Joseph doesn't say that, friend. His words are, "Not so, my father! This one is the firstborn; put your right hand on his head." (Genesis 48:18) He speaks up about the firstborn, and nothing about eyes comes out of his mouth.

explanations.answer: Ephraim is too young so bless him another day
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Joseph says, "Not so, my father! This one is the firstborn; put your right hand on his head." (Genesis 48:18) He's pointing at Manasseh, the firstborn. He doesn't ask for any other day.
Not this time, friend. Joseph tries to move the hand, but his father refuses. (Genesis 48:19) Israel says, "I know, my son, I know!" and keeps his right hand right where it is.
That's right, friend. The text says "his father refused." (Genesis 48:19) Israel keeps his right hand on Ephraim. Joseph pushes, and his father doesn't budge.

explanations.answer: He'll be greater and his offspring will become many nations
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Israel says Manasseh "shall become a people, and he too shall be great; nevertheless, his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his offspring shall become a multitude of nations." (Genesis 48:19) Manasseh gets a real blessing too. Ephraim's is just bigger.

explanations.answer: He'll serve Manasseh for the rest of his life
explanations.explanation: It goes the other way, friend. Israel says, "his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his offspring shall become a multitude of nations." (Genesis 48:19) Manasseh is blessed too, since he'll be a people and be great. Nobody's serving anybody here.

explanations.answer: He'll lead the whole family back to Canaan
explanations.explanation: That isn't in this blessing, friend. Israel says of Ephraim, "his younger brother shall be greater than he, and his offspring shall become a multitude of nations." (Genesis 48:19) It's about greatness and a multitude of nations. Leading the family back isn't mentioned.

Yes, friend. Israel says, "Look, I am about to die, but God will be with you and bring you back to the land of your fathers." (Genesis 48:21) He knows his time is short. And he points Joseph to what God will do.

It's true, friend. Israel says, "Look, I am about to die, but God will be with you and bring you back to the land of your fathers." (Genesis 48:21) Both halves are in the same verse. He's honest about dying and sure about God being with Joseph.

That's it, friend. Israel says, "I give the ridge of land that I took from the Amorites with my sword and bow." (Genesis 48:22) He gives it to Joseph as one who is above his brothers. That's a gift worth getting from your dad.
No sheep here, friend. Israel gives Joseph "the ridge of land that I took from the Amorites with my sword and bow." (Genesis 48:22) It's land he took, not animals. Sheep would be a different gift.

No cup, friend. Israel says, "I give the ridge of land that I took from the Amorites with my sword and bow." (Genesis 48:22) The gift is land. Joseph does have a silver cup in his own story, but that's not what this verse is about (Genesis 44:2).
